verdicts.why: Coming into being as a distinct thing is plain description; no attitude toward what forms.
Making or shaping something for a purpose is neutral craft language, as plain as 'make'.
Taking on a shape says nothing about whether the shape is welcome or not.
Forming an opinion or expectation is a plain mental act, with no judgement of the opinion or of the person holding it.
Giving up is a referent people disapprove of, but 'quit' itself is as plain as 'give up' or 'stop'; the disapproval lives in the derived 'quitter', not in this verb.
Leaving off a habit, place, or activity is stated without any view of whether one should.
Bringing something new into a setting is neutral; the word does not say whether the novelty is good or bad.
Presenting something to the public for the first time is a plain report of an event, not an opinion of it.
Putting a bill or motion before a body is procedural vocabulary with no attitude attached.
Supplying a preface is a neutral editorial act.
Inserting one thing into another is physical description in a formal register; register is not attitude.
Putting something into something else describes an action without judging it.
Being the precursor of something is a plain statement of sequence.
A formal contest is named neutrally, as 'game' or 'contest' would be.
An exact duplicate is a statement of sameness with no attitude toward either item.
Something that goes with or resembles another is a description of fit; any approval comes from the modifier ('good', 'unsuitable'), not from 'match'.
A person of equal standing is a statement of parity, and 'no match for' judges by comparison, not by the word itself.
A small stick for striking a flame is a concrete object name with nothing to judge.
A score needed to win is a sporting technicality, wholly neutral.
Moving upward is plain motion in a literary register; the register does not add an attitude toward the thing rising.
Getting to one's feet is described, not judged; 'arise' is merely a more formal 'stand up'.
Getting out of bed is a plain daily act; the old-fashioned register carries no approval or contempt.
Chosen over 'rebel' or 'revolt', 'arise' casts the rising as stirring and righteous, a people throwing off oppression rather than subjects breaking allegiance; the speaker sides with the risers.
Getting in contact with someone is neutral practical language.
Extending as far as a point is plain spatial description with no attitude toward what is reached.
